headline_marked: [[Anthropic's Claude Fable didn't win]] a real-world monorepo audit, highlighting multi-model pipeline need
headline: Anthropic's Claude Fable didn't win a real-world monorepo audit, highlighting multi-model pipeline need
summary: A real-world audit of Anthropic's Claude models found that even the top-tier Fable missed critical issues, underscoring the value of diverse AI tools.
details: A recent experiment audited a production monorepo using five Claude models, including the new Fable tier. The goal was to assess their performance on hard engineering work, not just benchmark scores.

The audit was conducted via CTRL NODE, using one agent per model tier to simulate a real-world team workflow. This approach aimed to provide principal-engineer level findings with file:line evidence and severity labels.

While Haiku's initial assessment appeared confident, cross-checking with Sonnet 4.6 revealed a factual error regarding lockfile validation in CI. This highlighted the importance of cross-verification.

Opus and Fable both achieved an A- grade but excelled in different areas. Opus identified design-level threats, while Fable focused on converting findings into a shippable backlog with effort/risk assessments.

Crucially, Fable failed to identify several issues that other models caught, such as TOCTOU, shell host defaults, and SSRF gaps. This gap demonstrates that Fable is not a standalone replacement for a multi-model pipeline.

The experiment concludes that model choice should be a workflow decision, not merely a pick based on the most expensive tier. Utilizing a diverse set of AI models can lead to more comprehensive and accurate results.

headline_marked: [[Local AI runtimes are part of your attack surface now]], requiring new security considerations for developers
headline: Local AI runtimes are part of your attack surface now, requiring new security considerations for developers
summary: The convenience of local AI tools like Docker Model Runner introduces new supply chain vulnerabilities and unauthenticated API risks to developer machines.
details: Local AI tools, often perceived as secure due to on-device processing, are adding new attack surfaces to developer machines. Docker's recent security fixes for its Model Runner highlight these emerging risks, including container-to-host code execution and SSRF vulnerabilities.

Docker Model Runner, designed to pull models from Docker Hub, OCI registries, and Hugging Face, serves them via OpenAI and Ollama-compatible APIs. While useful for integrating AI into development workflows, this functionality introduces significant trust boundaries on a single laptop.

The mental image of a simple, isolated local AI process is often too small. The runtime environment involves pulling artifacts, parsing metadata, and loading native code, creating a complex supply chain that mirrors traditional software dependencies.

Vulnerabilities like Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) in the OCI registry client demonstrate how old attack classes reappear in new contexts. On a developer machine, SSRF could expose internal registries, VPN-only services, localhost APIs, and local credentials.

The unauthenticated nature of the Docker Model Runner API, by default, allows any client on the same Docker network to pull, load, and run models. This makes the API a critical part of the container network and a potential entry point for malicious activity if not properly secured.

Modern developer machines are complex ecosystems of various tools, runtimes, and services. Local AI runtimes, despite their unique terminology, behave like other privileged developer services, demanding the same rigorous security thinking applied to other infrastructure.
